catalog_quote: 4. In vier- und fünfsilbigen wörtern fällt fortis auf die erste silbe und levis, resp. levior meistens auf jede folgende lange silbe und ausserdem levis oder levior auf die dritte und fünfte silbe, wenn die vierte silbe kurz ist, z. b.: ... 5. Wenn der musikalische accent auf der ersten silbe der grundton (sieh § 22) ist, wird der accent auf der ersten silbe wahrscheinlich (wie im schwedischen) etwas schwächer ... in vier- und fünfsilbigen wörtern: fortis — levis oder levior — fortis — levis oder levior — levissimus — levior ... Diese accentuirung (mit grundton-ters) ist nicht wie im schwedischen an gewisse wörter gebunden, sondern ist nur retorisch. § 21. Aus diesen auseinandersetzungen geht hervor, dass im Lulelappischen der hauptton auf die erste (bisweilen auf die erste und dritte) silbe fällt und dass ein nebenton auf jede folgende silbe fallen kann. Bei der besprechung der veränderungen, denen der schlussvokal des stammes und einige suffixe in gewissen fällen unterliegen, wird hier jedoch nur die erste, dritte und fünfte silbe accentuirt oder betont und die zweite und vierte silbe unaccentuirt oder unbetont genannt.

In vier- und fünfsilbigen wörtern fällt fortis auf die erste silbe und levis, resp. levior meistens auf jede folgende lange silbe und ausserdem levis oder levior auf die dritte und fünfte silbe, wenn die vierte silbe kurz ist [...] § 21. Bei der besprechung der veränderungen, denen der schlussvokal des stammes und einige suffixe in gewissen fällen unterliegen, wird hier jedoch nur die erste, dritte und fünfte silbe accentuirt oder betont und die zweite und vierte silbe unaccentuirt oder unbetont genannt.
new_statements.translation: 4. In four- and five-syllable words the fortis (main stress) falls on the first syllable and levis or levior (secondary stress) mostly on every following long syllable, and in addition levis or levior on the third and fifth syllable when the fourth syllable is short [...] § 21. From these discussions it follows that in Lule Lappish the main stress falls on the first (sometimes on the first and third) syllable and that a secondary stress can fall on every following syllable. In discussing the changes that the stem-final vowel and some suffixes undergo in certain cases, however, only the first, third and fifth syllables will here be called accented or stressed and the second and fourth syllables unaccented or unstressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (expiratory) stress is fixed on the word-initial syllable. Wiklund distinguishes four stress grades (fortis, levis, levior, levissimus): disyllables are fortis + levissimus/levis/levior depending on syllable length; in longer words secondary stresses fall on following long syllables and rhythmically on the 3rd and 5th syllables; monosyllabic function words are usually unstressed in connected speech. Corroborated verbatim by Wiklund 1901 Lärobok §17 p.12 ('Accenten ligger i lapskan alltid på ordets första stafvelse, hvarjämte i längre ord en eller flera biaccenter förekomma') and Collinder 1938 §141 p.43 for Gällivare Forest Saami ('Der hauptdruck ruht auf dem ersten lauttal'), §147 rhythmic odd-syllable secondary prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Graded secondary stresses (levis 'starker nebenton', levior 'schwacher nebenton'): in disyllables levis on a long second syllable after a short first syllable, levior when both syllables are long; in trisyllables levior on the 3rd when the 2nd is short, levis/levior on a long 2nd; in 4-5-syllable words levis/levior on each following long syllable and on the 3rd and 5th syllables when the 4th is short (§20.2-4). Wiklund 1901 §17: one or more 'biaccenter' in longer words; a long vowel in the 2nd or 4th syllable is pronounced with secondary accent. Collinder 1938 §§143-147: long syllables stronger than short ones of the same position; long 3rd syllable stronger than long 2nd/4th; general rhythmic tendency for odd-numbered syllables to be stronger.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Monosyllabic words are mostly unstressed (levissimus) in context (§20.1); (ii) the interrogative interjection J. mava / N.J. mavæ 'wie?' often has the main accent (or a very strong secondary) on the last syllable (§20.2 Anm.); (iii) with the rhetorical 'grundton–ters' pitch pattern the first-syllable accent is somewhat weaker and combined with levior/levis on the second syllable (§20.5, p.12: 'nur retorisch'); (iv) borrowed place/personal names (stókhól'ma, fórsbárja, viklúnta) and ködör've follow the fortis–levis pattern (§20.3 Anm.); (v) Wiklund 1901 §18 and Collinder 1938 §150: compounds whose first member is shortened take the main accent on the second member (tjas-ridne, kat-kieris; Collinder tjáj-lottie), otherwise main accent on the first member and secondary on the second.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the word accent ('Der wortaccent', §20) of the expiratory/stress accent, kept separate from the musical (pitch) accent treated in §§22-23; observation that monosyllables are unstressed refers to connected speech (example sentence). Data from Wiklund's 1885-86 and 1888 fieldwork in Jokkmokk and Gellivare (dialects S.J., N.J., S.G., N.G.).
new_statements.identity_note: Wiklund 1891 describes the Lule Saami ('Lule-lappisch') dialects of Jokkmokk and Gellivare parishes, Swedish Lule lappmark (S.J., N.J., S.G., N.G; he notes N.G. diverges toward Torne/North Saami and that the same dialects are spoken in adjacent Norway: S.J. in inner Folda, N.J. in Tysfjord) = Glottolog lule1254. Wiklund 1901 is a normalised pedagogical grammar explicitly of 'lulelapskan' (p.2). Collinder 1938 describes the Forest Saami dialect of Gällivare (waldlappisch), which Glottolog files under lule1254 but which some treat as a transitional Lule/North variety; its stress statement agrees (initial main stress, rhythmic odd-syllable secondary). All three use the older exonym 'lappisch/lapska' for Saami.

new_statements.quote: Accent. § 17. Accenten ligger i lapskan alltid på ordets första stafvelse, hvarjämte en eller flera biaccenter kunna förekomma, t. ex. kúltaláddat »röra vid»; pákåtállat »undervisa»; pákåtalái »han undervisade»; kúlåu »jag hör». En lång vokal i andra eller fjärde stafvelsen uttalas sålunda med biaccent. § 18. I sammansatta substantiv erhåller stundom den andra sammansättningsleden hufvudaccenten, hvarvid den första sammansättningsleden förkortas, t. ex.: tjas-rúdnē [...]; däremot t. ex. tjåhtsē-rássē »ogräs i åker»; hílla-káhkkō »kaka, gräddad på glöden» med hufvudaccent på den oförkortade första leden och biaccent på den andra.
new_statements.translation: Accent. §17. In Lappish the accent always lies on the first syllable of the word, alongside which one or more secondary accents may occur, e.g. kúltaláddat 'to touch'; pákåtállat 'to teach'; pákåtalái 'he taught'; kúlåu 'I hear'. A long vowel in the second or fourth syllable is thus pronounced with a secondary accent. §18. In compound nouns the second member of the compound sometimes receives the main accent, in which case the first member is shortened, e.g. tjas-rúdnē [...]; by contrast e.g. tjåhtsē-rássē 'weed in a field'; hílla-káhkkō 'cake baked on the embers' with main accent on the unshortened first member and secondary accent on the second.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word accent is always on the first syllable of the word (the book explicitly treats the form spoken in Lule lappmark). Secondary accents occur in longer words: the marked examples show by-accents on the third syllable (kúltaláddat, pákåtállat) and, when the second or fourth syllable has a long vowel, on that syllable (pákåtalái, kúlåu). In compound nouns whose first member is shortened, the main accent may instead fall on the (first syllable of the) second member; otherwise main accent on the first member and secondary on the second. Elsewhere (p. 14) 'betonad stafvelse (d. v. s. första stafvelsen)' equates the stressed syllable with the first syllable; §3 p. 9 adds that within diphthongs the 'hufvudtonvikt' is always on the first vowel, except that no simple rule can be given for ie and uö.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'en eller flera biaccenter kunna förekomma'; a long vowel in the 2nd or 4th syllable takes a secondary accent (pákåtalái, kúlåu); otherwise examples mark by-accent on the 3rd syllable (kúltaláddat, pákåtállat); in unshortened compounds the second member carries a by-accent (hílla-káhkkō).
new_statements.exceptions: §18: in compound nouns with a shortened first member the main accent sometimes falls on the second member (tjas-rúdnē, kåt-kíeris). §3: position of prominence inside the diphthongs ie, uö not rule-governed. No lexical exceptions to initial main accent in simplex words are mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: Wiklund 1915 describes 'lapska.. med särskild hänsyn till den form af detsamma, som talas i Lule lappmark' (preface, imprint spread Sida 8), i.e. Lule Saami of Lule lappmark (Gällivare/Jokkmokk; the book's own dialect list groups Tysfjord/Hamarøy/Folda in Norway with it). The opened copy is Umeå University Library's digitisation of the Nordkalottbibliotek exemplar of the same 1915 2nd revised edition as the listed HathiTrust/Harvard item.
